entries.label: idiom
entries.meaning: A long effort that needs patience and steady pacing, so you should not use up all your energy at the start.
entries.usage: Common advice about careers, studies, recovery, fitness and long campaigns, usually after *It's* or *This is*. It sounds encouraging and is often said to someone who is impatient or burning out. People sometimes reverse it, *a sprint, not a marathon*, for a short and intense push.
examples: Paying off debt is **a marathon, not a sprint**, so don't panic if progress feels slow.
Coach keeps reminding us that the season is **a marathon, not a sprint**.
Treat grad school like **a marathon, not a sprint**, or you'll burn out by your second year.

drill.sentence: Learning a language is {{a marathon, not a sprint}}, so ten minutes a day beats one long weekend session.
drill.hint: a long effort that needs steady pacing (a running image)

entries.related: *play the long game* — aim for long-term success; *slow and steady wins the race* — patience beats speed; *pace yourself* — don't use all your energy too early.

entries.label: idiom
entries.meaning: Still facing danger or difficulties, even though the situation has improved.
entries.usage: Common in medicine, economics, weather reports and sports: *We're not out of the woods yet*. It is almost always negative and often ends with *yet*. It sounds cautious: it admits progress but warns against relaxing too soon.
examples: The surgery went well, but the doctors say he's **not out of the woods** yet.
Inflation is falling, but economists warn that the economy is **not out of the woods**.
The team has won two straight, but they're still **not out of the woods** in the playoff race.

drill.sentence: The fire is mostly under control, but with strong winds expected tonight, the town is {{not out of the woods}} yet.
drill.hint: a forest image: the danger has not fully passed

entries.related: *on the mend* — recovering; *a close call* — a narrow escape; *home free* — sure to succeed now, the opposite.

entries.term: wait for the other shoe to drop
entries.label: idiom
entries.meaning: To wait nervously for a second bad event that you expect will follow a first one, or that seems sure to come after good luck.
entries.usage: Common in American conversation and news, usually in the progressive (*be waiting for the other shoe to drop*). It describes tension after bad news, or suspicion when things seem too good to be true. *The other shoe dropped* means the expected bad event finally happened.
examples: After the first round of layoffs, everyone in the office was **waiting for the other shoe to drop**.
The first date went so well that I kept **waiting for the other shoe to drop**.
Investors are **waiting for the other shoe to drop** after the bank's surprise loss.

drill.sentence: My landlord fixed the heater the same day I asked and even lowered my rent, so now I'm {{waiting for the other shoe to drop}}.
drill.hint: expecting the bad news that surely comes next (a footwear image)

entries.related: *brace yourself* — prepare for something unpleasant; *too good to be true* — so good that it seems suspicious; *the calm before the storm* — a quiet period before trouble.
entries.origin: From the image of hearing an upstairs neighbor drop one shoe on the floor and lying awake waiting for the second.

entries.label: idiom
entries.meaning: A call for everyone available to help, usually because of an emergency or an unusually large amount of work.
entries.usage: Used at work, in families and in organizations, usually as *It's all hands on deck*. It can also be an adjective: *an all-hands-on-deck moment*. Don't confuse it with *an all-hands*, which is a company-wide meeting.
examples: The restaurant got slammed after the game, so it was **all hands on deck** in the kitchen.
We're moving on Saturday, so it's **all hands on deck** — even the kids are packing boxes.
When the wildfire reached the valley, it was **all hands on deck** for every fire department in the county.

drill.sentence: Grandma's ninetieth birthday party is tomorrow and nothing is ready, so it's {{all hands on deck}}.
drill.hint: everyone has to help (a ship image)

entries.related: *pitch in* — help with a shared task; *a team effort* — success that depends on everyone; *an all-hands* — a company-wide meeting.
entries.origin: From sailing ships, where the order called every sailor (*hand*) up to the deck.

entries.label: idiom
entries.meaning: To make every possible effort and use every available resource to make something succeed.
entries.usage: Used about events, celebrations, campaigns and rescue efforts: *The city pulled out all the stops for the parade*. It's positive and suggests great effort or expense. The usual patterns are *pull out all the stops for* + event and *to* + verb.
entries.pattern: pull out all the stops for something / to do something
examples: My in-laws **pulled out all the stops** for our wedding, down to the live swing band.
The museum is **pulling out all the stops** for its hundredth anniversary, with free entry all weekend.
The hospital staff **pulled out all the stops** to save the premature twins.

drill.sentence: For Dad's retirement party, we {{pulled out all the stops}}: catering, a slideshow and a surprise visit from his old army buddies.
drill.hint: made every possible effort (an organ image; not *went all out*)

entries.related: *go all out* — make a great effort; *go the extra mile* — do more than expected; *spare no expense* — spend whatever is needed.
entries.origin: From the pipe organ: pulling out all the stops (the knobs that control the pipes) makes it play at full power.

entries.label: idiom
entries.meaning: A situation or thing that is likely to cause serious trouble soon if nothing is done about it.
entries.usage: Common in news, health and politics, often as a warning that action is urgent: *The pension system is a ticking time bomb*. It sounds alarming and dramatic, so it's typical of headlines and speeches.
examples: Untreated high blood pressure is **a ticking time bomb**, because it often has no symptoms.
Engineers warn that the old dam above the town is **a ticking time bomb**.
The electrician took one look at our attic wiring and called it **a ticking time bomb**.

drill.sentence: With rents rising and wages flat, the city's housing situation is {{a ticking time bomb}}.
drill.hint: a danger that will go off soon — a clock image (not *a disaster waiting to happen*)

entries.related: *a disaster waiting to happen* — similar, plainer; *a powder keg* — a tense situation that could suddenly turn violent; *a canary in the coal mine* — an early warning sign.

entries.label: idiom
entries.meaning: Tricks or misleading explanations that hide the truth or create a false impression, especially of success.
entries.usage: Critical, and common in politics, business and finance: *The turnaround was all smoke and mirrors*. It often follows *all*, *just* or *nothing but*. It suggests deliberate deception, so it's a strong charge.
examples: Critics say the new budget is all **smoke and mirrors**, designed to hide a huge deficit.
The company's 'record profits' were mostly **smoke and mirrors**: one-time sales and creative accounting.
His famous charm is nothing but **smoke and mirrors**; once you get to know him, he isn't very kind.

drill.sentence: The diet company's 'before and after' photos were just {{smoke and mirrors}}, with clever lighting and a lot of editing.
drill.hint: tricks that create a false impression (a magic-show image)

entries.related: *a smoke screen* — something used to hide what you're really doing; *window dressing* — something done to look good, with little substance; *sleight of hand* — skillful deception.
entries.origin: From stage magic, where magicians use smoke and mirrors to create illusions.

entries.label: idiom
entries.meaning: To make a bad situation, conflict or strong feeling even worse, often by saying or doing something provocative.
entries.usage: Common in news and everyday arguments, often with *only* or *just*: *His comments only added fuel to the fire*. *Pour fuel on the fire* and *add fuel to the flames* are common variants. It is about a conflict or anger growing, unlike *add insult to injury*.
examples: The singer's angry reply **added fuel to the fire**, and the online feud went on for weeks.
Don't bring up his ex while they're arguing; you'll just **add fuel to the fire**.
A leaked memo **added fuel to the fire** as the nurses' strike entered its third week.

drill.sentence: The two neighbors were already fighting about the fence, and calling the police only {{added fuel to the fire}}.
drill.hint: made the conflict worse — a flame image (not *fanned the flames*)

entries.related: *fan the flames* — encourage strong feelings, often on purpose; *add insult to injury* — make things worse for someone already hurt; *smooth things over* — calm a conflict, the opposite.

entries.label: idiom
entries.meaning: To make a bad situation even worse for someone who has already been harmed or treated unfairly.
entries.usage: Very common as an opening phrase, *to add insult to injury*, which introduces a second, worse thing. It can be serious or humorous, and the second problem is often small but humiliating. Unlike *add fuel to the fire*, it is about one person's bad luck, not a growing conflict.
examples: My flight was canceled and, **to add insult to injury**, the airline lost my bag.
The team lost in overtime, and then their bus broke down on the way home — talk about **adding insult to injury**.
The company laid off two hundred workers and then **added insult to injury** by cutting their severance.

drill.sentence: I got a parking ticket while I was at the dentist, and {{to add insult to injury}}, it started pouring on my walk back.
drill.hint: a phrase about being hurt and then mocked (not *to make matters worse*)

entries.related: *to make matters worse* — plainer; *rub salt in the wound* — make someone's pain worse, often on purpose; *add fuel to the fire* — make a conflict worse.
entries.origin: Traced to a fable by the Roman writer Phaedrus: a bald man hits his own head while trying to kill a fly that bit him, and the fly mocks him.

entries.label: idiom
entries.meaning: A sudden, unpleasant discovery that a situation is much worse or harder than you believed.
entries.usage: Common in conversation and journalism, either as a warning, *be in for a rude awakening*, or as *get* or *have a rude awakening*. *Rude* here means sudden and harsh, not impolite. As a warning to someone naive, it can sound a little smug.
examples: If you think owning a dog is easy, you're in for **a rude awakening**.
My first electricity bill in the new apartment was **a rude awakening**.
The early loss was **a rude awakening** for a team that expected to win the title easily.

drill.sentence: Many new graduates get {{a rude awakening}} when they see how much rent costs in big cities.
drill.hint: a sudden, unpleasant discovery (not *a reality check* or *a wake-up call*)

entries.related: *a reality check* — a reminder of the true situation, often useful; *a wake-up call* — an event that warns you to change; *disillusioned* — disappointed after learning the truth.

entries.label: idiom
entries.meaning: To keep something secret for a period of time, usually until an official announcement.
entries.usage: Common about products, plans, deals, surprises and celebrity news, often in the passive: *The details are being kept under wraps*. It suggests a planned reveal later, which makes it different from *hide* or *cover up*. The object usually comes between *keep* and *under wraps*.
entries.pattern: keep something under wraps; be kept under wraps
examples: The company is **keeping** the new phone **under wraps** until its launch in September.
We're **keeping** the pregnancy **under wraps** until after the first trimester.
The city **kept** the stadium deal **under wraps** for months before announcing it.

drill.sentence: The surprise party is next Saturday, so let's keep it {{under wraps}} until then.
drill.hint: hidden for now — a covering image (not *quiet* or *secret*)

entries.related: *keep something quiet* — not talk about it; *hush-hush* — informal, secret; *leak* — reveal secret information, the opposite.

entries.term: get the short end of the stick
entries.label: idiom
entries.meaning: To get the worse part of a deal or situation, especially when someone else gets the better part.
entries.usage: Common in American conversation as a complaint about unfair deals, chores, schedules and family arrangements; *end up with the short end of the stick* is also common. It sounds aggrieved but casual. Don't confuse it with British *get the wrong end of the stick*, which means to misunderstand.
examples: In the divorce, he kept the house, and she **got the short end of the stick**.
Small farmers often **get the short end of the stick** in big trade deals.
When the office moved, our team **ended up with the short end of the stick**: no windows and a broken AC.

drill.sentence: Whenever we split a pizza, my older brothers grab the big slices, and I {{get the short end of the stick}}.
drill.hint: end up with the worse part of the deal (a wooden-rod image)

entries.related: *draw the short straw* — be chosen, by chance, to do an unpleasant task; *get the wrong end of the stick* — British, misunderstand something; *lose out* — miss a benefit that others get.

entries.term: the writing is on the wall
entries.label: idiom
entries.meaning: There are clear signs that something bad, such as failure or the end of something, is going to happen.
entries.usage: Common in news, business and personal life, often with *for* + the thing that will fail: *The writing is on the wall for cable TV*. *See the writing on the wall* means to recognize the signs, often in time to act. Americans also say *the handwriting is on the wall*.
examples: When the company froze hiring and canceled the holiday party, **the writing was on the wall**.
She **saw the writing on the wall** and started looking for a new job before the layoffs.
For the town's last video rental store, **the writing had been on the wall** for years.

drill.sentence: Their fights were getting worse every week, and by spring {{the writing was on the wall}}: they were going to break up.
drill.hint: a biblical image: obvious signs of a coming end

entries.related: *a canary in the coal mine* — an early warning sign; *the beginning of the end* — the start of a final decline; *see it coming* — expect something before it happens.
entries.origin: From the Book of Daniel, where a mysterious hand writes a warning of doom on the wall of King Belshazzar's palace.

entries.term: cross that bridge when you come to it
entries.label: idiom
entries.meaning: To deal with a possible problem only if and when it actually happens, instead of worrying about it now.
entries.usage: Common in conversation as calming advice, usually with *we'll* or *I'll* in front, and often shortened to *cross that bridge later*. It can sound wise or slightly evasive, depending on whether the problem should really be planned for.
examples: 'What if the baby comes early?' 'We'll **cross that bridge when we come to it**.'
I don't know how we'll pay for college yet, but I'll **cross that bridge when I come to it**.
Asked whether the bakery would ever open a second location, the owner said she'd **cross that bridge when she came to it**.

drill.sentence: Don't stress about what to do if it rains on the wedding day; we'll {{cross that bridge when we come to it}}.
drill.hint: deal with that problem only if it happens (a river image)

entries.related: *play it by ear* — decide as you go; *don't borrow trouble* — don't worry about problems before they happen; *worry about that later* — plainer.

entries.label: idiom
entries.meaning: To cause trouble or upset a stable situation by challenging the way things are done.
entries.usage: Usually in the negative, as in *don't rock the boat*. Common at work, in families and in politics, about people who stay quiet to keep the peace. It can also be approving: *Sometimes you need to rock the boat*.
examples: I didn't love the new schedule, but I didn't want to **rock the boat** in my first month.
Everyone avoided politics at dinner; nobody wanted to **rock the boat** on Grandma's birthday.
The neighborhood association had been peaceful for years, and the board didn't want to **rock the boat** with new parking rules.

drill.sentence: Things are finally calm between my parents, so please don't {{rock the boat}} by bringing up the inheritance again.
drill.hint: disturb the calm (a sailing image; not *make waves*)

entries.related: *make waves* — cause trouble or attract attention; *stir the pot* — cause conflict on purpose; *upset the apple cart* — spoil a plan or arrangement.

entries.label: idiom
entries.meaning: To deliberately cause trouble, tension or argument between people, often for fun or attention.
entries.usage: Common in American conversation, reality TV and social media talk about gossip and drama: *He's just stirring the pot*. Unlike *rock the boat*, it suggests a deliberate and sometimes mischievous intent. A person who does this is a *pot-stirrer*.
examples: My aunt loves to **stir the pot** at family dinners by bringing up old fights.
Some commentators just **stir the pot** online to get more clicks.
Reality shows always cast at least one person whose job is to **stir the pot**.

drill.sentence: I know you're only joking, but telling Mike that Dave called his car ugly is just {{stirring the pot}}.
drill.hint: deliberately causing trouble between people (a cooking image)

entries.related: *rock the boat* — upset a stable situation, often by speaking up; *add fuel to the fire* — make a conflict worse; *drama* — informal, conflict between people.

entries.label: idiom
entries.meaning: To try extremely hard to help or please someone, often more than they deserve.
entries.usage: Common in conversation and business, as *bend over backwards to* + verb or *for* + person. It usually praises the helper, but it can also suggest that the effort was not appreciated. *Lean over backwards* is a less common variant.
entries.pattern: bend over backwards to do something / for someone
examples: The hotel staff **bent over backwards** to make my parents' anniversary special.
We **bent over backwards** for that client, and they still went with a cheaper firm.
Our neighbors **bent over backwards** to help us after the fire.

drill.sentence: My grandmother would {{bend over backwards}} for anyone who knocked on her door.
drill.hint: make huge efforts to help (a gymnast image; not *go out of her way*)

entries.related: *go out of your way* — make a special effort; *go the extra mile* — do more than expected; *pull out all the stops* — use every resource to succeed.

entries.label: idiom
entries.meaning: To take a risk, especially by supporting someone or saying something that others might criticize.
entries.usage: Common at work, in politics and between friends, often with *for* + person: *She stuck her neck out for me*. It stresses a risk to your reputation or position. It's also used before a bold prediction.
examples: I **stuck my neck out** to get you this job, so please don't be late.
None of the other neighbors would **stick their necks out** and testify about the noise.
I'll **stick my neck out** and say the Bears will make the playoffs this year.

drill.sentence: When the other parents complained about the new music teacher, Lisa {{stuck her neck out}} and defended him at the meeting.
drill.hint: risked criticism by backing someone (a body-part image; not *went out on a limb*)

entries.related: *go out on a limb* — take a risk by supporting an idea or person; *put yourself on the line* — risk your reputation or safety; *play it safe* — the opposite.

entries.label: idiom
entries.meaning: To firmly insist on something, or refuse to allow it, using your authority.
entries.usage: Common about parents, partners, bosses and officials, often with *finally* and with *about* or *on* + topic. It sounds firm but not aggressive, and it usually ends a discussion. Especially in British English, it can also mean to make a car go faster.
examples: After the third broken window, Dad **put his foot down**: no more baseball in the yard.
The principal **put her foot down** on phones in class.
The CEO finally **put his foot down** and canceled the project that kept missing deadlines.

drill.sentence: My kids wanted a third pet, but I {{put my foot down}} — two cats are more than enough.
drill.hint: firmly refused (a body-part image; not *drew the line*)

entries.related: *draw the line* — set a limit; *lay down the law* — tell people strictly what to do; *stand your ground* — refuse to change your position.

entries.term: put your foot in your mouth
entries.label: idiom
entries.meaning: To say something embarrassing or tactless by accident, which offends or upsets someone.
entries.usage: Common in American conversation, often about yourself as a kind of apology. The comic tone makes it a gentle way to admit a mistake. British speakers more often say *put your foot in it*, and someone who does this a lot has *foot-in-mouth disease*.
examples: I asked her when the baby was due, and she wasn't pregnant. I really **put my foot in my mouth**.
The talk-show host **put his foot in his mouth** with a joke about his guest's age.
In the interview, Tom **put his foot in his mouth** by complaining about his old boss.

drill.sentence: I made fun of the terrible singer, then found out she was the host's daughter. I totally {{put my foot in my mouth}}.
drill.hint: said something tactless by accident (a body-part image, the American form)

entries.related: *put your foot in it* — British version; *a faux pas* — a social mistake, formal; *stick your foot in your mouth* — same meaning, American.

entries.label: idiom
entries.meaning: Overwhelmed with work and falling behind, or lost in too many small details.
entries.usage: The busy sense comes from restaurant slang: *We're in the weeds on table six*. In meetings, *get into the weeds* means to go into too much detail, often with *let's not*. Both uses are American and casual.
examples: Saturday night was chaos; by eight o'clock the whole kitchen was **in the weeds**.
Let's not get **into the weeds** on the budget today; we just need the big picture.
The ER nurse was so **in the weeds** that she never got a lunch break.

drill.sentence: Sorry I didn't call back — I've been {{in the weeds}} with the move and haven't had a minute to myself.
drill.hint: overwhelmed (a garden image; not *swamped* or *slammed*)

entries.related: *swamped* — have too much work; *bogged down* — slowed by problems or details; *the big picture* — the overall view.

entries.label: idiom
entries.meaning: An unfair campaign to find and punish people, often for their opinions, driven more by public pressure than by evidence.
entries.usage: Common in politics and news, especially as a defense: people under investigation call it *a witch hunt* to suggest it is unfair. *A political witch hunt* is a frequent phrase. It's a strong, emotional term, so neutral reporting usually presents it as someone's claim.
examples: The company's founder called the regulators' investigation **a witch hunt** and insisted he'd done nothing wrong.
After the leak, management launched **a witch hunt** to find out who had talked to the press.
The online pile-on turned into **a witch hunt**, and an innocent man lost his job.

drill.sentence: After the vase broke, Mom started {{a witch hunt}}, questioning each of us kids one by one.
drill.hint: an unfair search for someone to blame (a Salem image; not *an investigation*)

entries.related: *a smear campaign* — spreading false claims to damage someone; *McCarthyism* — the US anti-communist hunts of the 1950s; *a scapegoat* — someone unfairly blamed for others' faults.
entries.origin: From the witch trials of early modern Europe and colonial America, such as the Salem trials of 1692.

entries.label: idiom
entries.meaning: A person or thing that attracts criticism, anger or controversy, often more than others who are involved.
entries.usage: Common in American political and sports journalism, in the pattern *a lightning rod for* + criticism / controversy / anger. It's neutral to slightly sympathetic and suggests the person gets more blame than others. British English calls the device a *lightning conductor*.
entries.pattern: a lightning rod for + criticism / controversy / anger
examples: The airline's CEO became **a lightning rod** for anger over the holiday flight cancellations.
The quarterback is **a lightning rod** for criticism whenever the team loses.
The new bike lanes have become **a lightning rod** for drivers frustrated with traffic.

drill.sentence: Once the new school uniform policy started, the vice principal became {{a lightning rod}} for complaints from parents.
drill.hint: the one who attracts everyone's complaints (a storm image; not *a target*)

entries.related: *a scapegoat* — someone unfairly blamed; *a punching bag* — someone who is constantly attacked; *a hot-button issue* — a topic that causes strong feelings.

entries.label: idiom
entries.meaning: A single issue, question or quality that is used to judge whether someone or something is acceptable.
entries.usage: Common in politics and journalism, in the patterns *a litmus test for* + people and *a litmus test of* + quality. It can be critical when the test is too narrow: *Loyalty shouldn't be a litmus test for hiring*. In casual talk it's a personal rule for judging people.
entries.pattern: a litmus test for + people / of + quality
examples: For many car buyers, the length of the warranty is **a litmus test** of how much a brand trusts its own cars.
How someone treats the waiter is my **litmus test** on a first date.
Some coaches use the first practice of the season as **a litmus test** of a player's attitude.

drill.sentence: For my dad, a firm handshake was {{a litmus test}} of a person's character.
drill.hint: a single sign used to judge — a chemistry image (not the *acid* version)

entries.related: *the acid test* — a final, decisive test of whether something works; *a yardstick* — a standard for comparison; *a dealbreaker* — something that makes you reject an option.
entries.origin: From chemistry, where litmus paper turns red in an acid and blue in a base.

entries.label: idiom
entries.meaning: To argue about very small differences or details that do not really matter.
entries.usage: Usually critical, and often in the progressive or with *let's not*. Common in debates, legal arguments, family disagreements and at work. Speakers also admit it: *I know I'm splitting hairs, but …*; the noun is *hair-splitting*.
examples: Whether it's 'mostly done' or 'almost done' doesn't matter; you're just **splitting hairs**.
The lawyers spent an hour **splitting hairs** over the meaning of 'reasonable.'
Technically, a tomato is a fruit, but at the grocery store that's **splitting hairs**.

drill.sentence: It doesn't matter whether we leave at six fifty-five or seven — let's not {{split hairs}}.
drill.hint: argue over tiny differences (not *quibble* or *nitpick*)

entries.related: *nitpick* — criticize tiny details; *quibble* — argue about something small; *a distinction without a difference* — a difference that doesn't matter.

entries.label: idiom
entries.meaning: A decision to believe in or trust something without proof, accepting the risk that you might be wrong.
entries.usage: Common about career moves, relationships, investments and religion, with *take*, *make* or *require*. It's usually positive about courage. In an argument it can criticize a weak step in reasoning: *That conclusion requires a big leap of faith*.
examples: Quitting my job to open a bakery was **a leap of faith**, but I don't regret it.
Adopting a dog you've only seen in an online photo takes **a leap of faith**.
Handing your car keys to a sixteen-year-old for the first time is **a leap of faith** for any parent.

drill.sentence: We'd only known each other three months when we moved in together; it was {{a leap of faith}}, but it worked out.
drill.hint: a decision based on trust, not proof (a jumping image; not *a gamble*)

entries.related: *take the plunge* — finally do something risky; *a shot in the dark* — a guess with little information; *blind faith* — trust without question, often critical.

entries.label: idiom
entries.meaning: The moment when a series of small changes suddenly causes a large and often irreversible change.
entries.usage: Common in news, science and business, with *reach*, *hit* or *pass a tipping point*. It became popular after Malcolm Gladwell's book *The Tipping Point* (2000) and is frequent in writing about climate. In everyday talk it often means the moment you finally decide to act.
examples: Scientists warn that the ice sheet could pass **a tipping point** within decades.
The third noise complaint in a week was **the tipping point**; we finally moved.
Electric cars may be nearing **a tipping point** as prices keep falling.

drill.sentence: For years my dad ignored his back pain, but missing his grandson's soccer game was {{the tipping point}} that got him to see a doctor.
drill.hint: the moment small pressures finally added up to a big change — a balance image (not *the last straw*)

entries.related: *the last straw* — the final problem that makes you lose patience; *a turning point* — a moment of important change; *critical mass* — the amount needed for something to keep going on its own.

entries.label: idiom
entries.meaning: A situation in which one problem causes another, which then makes the first problem worse, so the pattern keeps repeating.
entries.usage: Common in talk about health, money and social problems: *a vicious cycle of poverty*, *break the vicious cycle*, *trapped in a vicious cycle*. British English more often says *a vicious circle*. The positive opposite is *a virtuous cycle*.
examples: Doctors say chronic pain and poor sleep can feed each other in **a vicious cycle**.
High-interest loans trap many families in **a vicious cycle** of debt.
When a team keeps losing, fans stop coming, the money dries up, and the best players leave: **a vicious cycle**.

drill.sentence: I eat junk food when I'm stressed, then feel guilty, which stresses me out even more; it's {{a vicious cycle}}.
drill.hint: a loop where each problem makes the next one worse (the American form)

entries.related: *a vicious circle* — British version; *a downward spiral* — a situation that keeps getting worse; *a virtuous cycle* — the positive opposite.

entries.term: damned if you do, damned if you don't
entries.label: idiom
entries.meaning: Said when every possible choice will lead to criticism or a bad result.
entries.usage: Common in conversation and commentary about leaders, parents, referees and anyone in a no-win position. The pronoun changes with the subject (*I'm damned if I do, damned if I don't*), and it often expresses sympathy for the person deciding. Some people hear *damned* as mildly rude, so it's avoided in very formal settings.
examples: If the diner raises prices, regulars complain; if not, it loses money. The owner is **damned if she does, damned if she doesn't**.
Every call a referee makes leaves someone furious; you're **damned if you do, damned if you don't**.
With teenagers, parents are **damned if they do, damned if they don't**: ask questions and you're nosy; don't, and you don't care.

drill.sentence: If I invite my dad's girlfriend to the wedding, Mom will be upset; if I don't, Dad will. I'm {{damned if I do, damned if I don't}}.
drill.hint: a phrase meaning every choice gets me blamed (not *in a no-win situation*)

entries.related: *a no-win situation* — every outcome is bad; *between a rock and a hard place* — facing two bad options; *a catch-22* — a trap created by contradictory rules.

entries.label: idiom
entries.meaning: A desperate last attempt that has very little chance of success.
entries.usage: Common in American sports talk, politics, business and law, often as an adjective: *a Hail Mary pass*, *a Hail Mary appeal*. It's casual and suggests the situation is almost lost. Because it comes from a Catholic prayer, it's always capitalized.
examples: With two seconds left, the quarterback threw **a Hail Mary** into the end zone.
The company's last-minute merger offer looked like **a Hail Mary** to avoid bankruptcy.
Sending my résumé straight to the CEO was **a Hail Mary**, but she actually called me back.

drill.sentence: Our handwritten apology to the neighbors was {{a Hail Mary}}, but they actually dropped the noise complaint.
drill.hint: a desperate last try — a football term named after a prayer (not *a long shot*)

entries.related: *a long shot* — something unlikely to succeed; *a last-ditch effort* — a final, desperate attempt; *a shot in the dark* — a guess with little information.
entries.origin: Named after the Catholic prayer; the football sense became famous after Roger Staubach's winning pass in a 1975 playoff game.

entries.label: idiom
entries.meaning: To improve your performance or effort to meet a higher standard or to keep up with competition.
entries.usage: Common in sports, work, school and dating, as advice or a challenge, often with *need to* or *have to*. It's informal and motivating, but from a boss it can sound pushy. *Up your game* means the same, and *raise your game* is more British.
entries.pattern: step up your / his / our / its game
examples: If we want to make the playoffs, our defense has to **step up its game**.
My sister's cooking is amazing; I really need to **step up my game**.
Our new competitor offers free shipping, so we'll have to **step up our game**.

drill.sentence: My friend's dog knows twenty tricks, and mine only knows 'sit.' I need to {{step up my game}}.
drill.hint: improve to meet a higher standard (not *up* or *raise*)

entries.related: *up your game* — same meaning; *rise to the occasion* — perform well when it matters; *pull your socks up* — British, start working harder.

entries.label: idiom
entries.meaning: To give up and admit defeat, usually after trying for a while and realizing you cannot succeed.
entries.usage: Common in sports, business, politics and personal goals. It suggests a reluctant but realistic decision rather than cowardice. The tone is neutral to slightly sad.
examples: After three failed attempts to fix the dishwasher myself, I **threw in the towel** and called a plumber.
The startup **threw in the towel** after it couldn't raise more money.
With their team down by thirty at halftime, half the fans **threw in the towel** and headed for the parking lot.

drill.sentence: I tried to learn the violin at forty, but after a year of terrible sounds, I {{threw in the towel}}.
drill.hint: admitted defeat and stopped (a boxing image; not *gave up*)

entries.related: *call it quits* — stop doing something, often by choice; *give up* — plainer; *hang in there* — keep going, the opposite advice.
entries.origin: From boxing, where a trainer throws a towel into the ring to stop a fight their boxer is losing.

entries.term: the deck is stacked against someone
entries.label: idiom
entries.meaning: Conditions are unfairly arranged so that someone is very likely to fail, whatever they do.
entries.usage: Common in American politics, sports and personal stories about inequality. Variants include *with the deck stacked against them* and *a stacked deck*. It expresses sympathy for the disadvantaged side and often anger at the system.
examples: Kids from poor neighborhoods often feel that **the deck is stacked against them**.
With **the deck stacked against her**, the young lawyer still won the case.
Small bookstores say **the deck is stacked against** them when online giants can sell books below cost.

drill.sentence: With no car, no savings and a criminal record, my cousin knew {{the deck was stacked against}} him in his job search.
drill.hint: a card-game phrase for an unfair system (not *the odds*)

entries.related: *the odds are against someone* — success is unlikely, but not necessarily unfair; *an uphill battle* — a very hard struggle; *a level playing field* — fair conditions, the opposite.
entries.origin: From card games, where a cheater secretly arranges (stacks) the cards in the deck.

entries.label: idiom
entries.meaning: To run into an unexpected problem that stops or slows progress.
entries.usage: Common in news, work updates and everyday talk, often with *over* or *with* + the cause: *The deal hit a snag over pricing*. It plays down the problem and suggests it can probably be solved. *Run into a snag* and *hit a bit of a snag* are common variants.
examples: Our kitchen remodel **hit a snag** when the contractor found mold behind the wall.
Peace talks **hit a snag** over the question of borders.
We've **hit a bit of a snag** with the visa application, so the trip might be delayed.

drill.sentence: We planned to drive to the lake on Friday, but we {{hit a snag}}: the car wouldn't start.
drill.hint: a short phrase for running into an unexpected problem (not *ran into trouble*)

entries.related: *a bump in the road* — a small problem that slows progress; *hit a wall* — reach a point where you cannot continue; *a hiccup* — a small, brief problem.

entries.label: idiom
entries.meaning: At a point where an important choice must be made that will shape the future.
entries.usage: Common in serious writing and personal talk about people, careers, countries and industries; *stand at a crossroads* is also common. It sounds thoughtful and a little dramatic. *Crossroads* ends in *-s* even when it means one place.
examples: At forty-five, with the kids in college, I felt like I was **at a crossroads**.
The country is **at a crossroads**: it can reform its pension system now or face a crisis later.
After the injury, the young pitcher was **at a crossroads** — rehab or retirement.

drill.sentence: After graduation, Maya was {{at a crossroads}}: take the job in Seattle or stay home with her sick mother.
drill.hint: facing a big choice about her future (a road image; not *torn*)

entries.related: *a fork in the road* — a point where you must choose between two paths; *a turning point* — a moment when things change; *on the fence* — undecided.

entries.label: idiom
entries.meaning: To lose energy, enthusiasm or momentum before you finish something.
entries.usage: Common about people, campaigns, economies and projects: *The recovery is running out of steam*. It suggests a gradual slowdown rather than a sudden failure. *Lose steam* means the same, and *pick up steam* is the opposite.
examples: I started the marathon too fast and **ran out of steam** after mile eighteen.
The protest movement **ran out of steam** by the end of the summer.
We were going to paint the whole house, but we **ran out of steam** after the kitchen.

drill.sentence: The kids were wild all morning, but by bedtime they'd finally {{run out of steam}}.
drill.hint: a train-engine image: no energy left (not *worn themselves out*)

entries.related: *lose steam* — slow down gradually; *burn out* — become exhausted from too much work; *run its course* — continue until it ends naturally.
entries.origin: From steam engines, which slow down and stop when they lose steam pressure.

entries.label: idiom
entries.meaning: Known to a person and receiving some of their attention, as something to consider or watch.
entries.usage: Common at work and in conversation, often in questions and in the negative: *not on my radar*. *Put something on someone's radar* means to make them aware of it. *Fly under the radar* means to avoid attention.
entries.pattern: on my / your / their radar; put something on someone's radar
examples: Our accountant put the new tax rule **on our radar** back in January, so we were ready.
Is the school fundraiser **on your radar**? It's next Saturday.
College coaches started calling once he got **on their radar** as a sophomore.

drill.sentence: Honestly, retirement savings weren't even {{on my radar}} until I turned forty.
drill.hint: something I was aware of and watching (a tracking-screen image; not *on my mind*)

entries.related: *fly under the radar* — avoid notice; *on the back burner* — postponed; *keep tabs on* — watch something closely.

entries.label: idiom
entries.meaning: Being planned, prepared or developed, and expected to happen or appear soon.
entries.usage: Common in business, government and media about products, projects, laws, sequels and changes: *More price increases are in the pipeline*. *Already in the pipeline* means the work has started. It's neutral; in casual speech people also say *in the works*.
examples: The studio has two more sequels **in the pipeline**.
The city says a new bike-share program is **in the pipeline** for next spring.
So, anything fun **in the pipeline** for the summer?

drill.sentence: My aunt has three grandchildren already and another one {{in the pipeline}}, due in March.
drill.hint: expected soon, as if moving through a tube (not *on the way* or *in the works*)

entries.related: *in the works* — being planned or prepared, more informal; *on the horizon* — likely to happen in the future; *on the back burner* — postponed.

entries.label: idiom
entries.meaning: A profound and lasting change in attitudes, policies or conditions.
entries.usage: Common in journalism, politics and business, usually as *a sea change in* + noun. It sounds a little formal and implies a deep transformation, so using it for small adjustments sounds like hype. It's often paired with *attitudes*, *opinion* and *policy*.
entries.pattern: a sea change in + attitudes / opinion / policy
examples: There's been **a sea change** in how Americans think about working from home since 2020.
Smartphones caused **a sea change** in how people shop and pay.
Moving from Houston to rural Maine was **a sea change** for our whole family.

drill.sentence: Ten years ago nobody in my town recycled; now almost everyone does. It's been {{a sea change}}.
drill.hint: a deep, lasting transformation (a Shakespeare phrase)

entries.related: *a paradigm shift* — a basic change in how something is understood, more academic; *a turning point* — a single moment of change; *a U-turn* — a complete reversal of policy.
entries.origin: From Shakespeare's *The Tempest*, where Ariel sings that a drowned man has suffered 'a sea-change into something rich and strange.'

entries.label: idiom
entries.meaning: A person who has not yet worked on or seen something, and who can therefore notice problems that others missed.
entries.usage: Common at work, in writing and in problem-solving, often when asking a colleague for help: *Could you give this a fresh pair of eyes?* It's polite and modest. *Fresh eyes* and *a new pair of eyes* mean the same.
examples: Can you read my cover letter? I need **a fresh pair of eyes** on it.
The cold case was solved after a new detective brought **a fresh pair of eyes** to it.
After two days staring at the same bug, I asked a coworker for **a fresh pair of eyes**.

drill.sentence: My sister spotted the typo on the wedding invitations in seconds; sometimes you just need {{a fresh pair of eyes}}.
drill.hint: someone new who can spot what you missed (not *a second opinion*)

entries.related: *a second opinion* — another expert's view, especially in medicine; *a sounding board* — someone you test ideas on; *too close to something* — too involved to see it clearly.

entries.label: idiom
entries.meaning: To finally tell the truth about something you have hidden, especially something you did wrong.
entries.usage: Common in conversation and news, usually with *about* + the secret or *to* + the person, and often with *finally*. It suggests relief or outside pressure after a period of hiding. It's informal but fine in journalism: *The cyclist came clean about doping*.
examples: My brother finally **came clean** about crashing Dad's car.
The company only **came clean** about the data breach after reporters found out.
If you **come clean** to your teacher now, the punishment will probably be lighter.

drill.sentence: After weeks of pretending she was still in school, Emma {{came clean}} to her parents and told them she'd dropped out.
drill.hint: finally told the truth (not *confessed* or *fessed up*)

entries.related: *own up to* — admit a mistake; *fess up* — informal, confess; *spill the beans* — reveal a secret, often by accident.

entries.label: idiom
entries.meaning: To report wrongdoing inside an organization, such as fraud or safety violations, to the authorities or the public.
entries.usage: Common in news, law and business, in the pattern *blow the whistle on* + person, company or practice. The person who does it is a *whistleblower*. It usually sounds brave and approving, although insiders may see it as betrayal.
entries.pattern: blow the whistle on + person / company / practice
examples: An accountant **blew the whistle on** the company's fake sales numbers.
A nurse **blew the whistle on** unsafe staffing levels at the hospital.
My little sister **blew the whistle on** our plan to sneak out after midnight.

drill.sentence: A former coach {{blew the whistle on}} the university's athletic department, which had been paying recruits in cash.
drill.hint: reported the wrongdoing in — a referee image (not *exposed*)

entries.related: *whistleblower* — the person who reports; *snitch on* / *rat on* — inform on someone, negative; *leak* — pass secret information to the media.

entries.term: put your money where your mouth is
entries.label: idiom
entries.meaning: To show that you really believe what you say by acting on it, especially by spending or risking your own money.
entries.usage: Often a challenge to someone who talks a lot, especially in politics, sports bets and business. It can also be praise for someone who acted on their words. The pronouns change with the subject: *put their money where their mouth is*.
examples: If you're so sure the Yankees will win, **put your money where your mouth is** and bet me twenty bucks.
The CEO **put her money where her mouth is** and gave up her bonus to save jobs.
Lots of companies praise working parents, but few **put their money where their mouth is** with real help for childcare.

drill.sentence: My neighbor kept saying the park needed more trees, so he {{put his money where his mouth was}} and paid for ten of them.
drill.hint: backed his words with action and cash

entries.related: *walk the walk* — act as you say others should; *talk is cheap* — words alone mean little; *put up or shut up* — prove it or stop talking, rude.

entries.label: idiom
entries.meaning: To follow the official rules, policy or opinion of a group, even if you personally disagree.
entries.usage: Common in politics, the military and workplaces, often as *toe the party line*. It's usually slightly critical, suggesting obedience rather than independent thinking. Typical patterns are *refuse to toe the line* and *be expected to toe the line*.
examples: Most senators **toed the party line** and voted against the bill.
New employees are expected to **toe the line** for their first year.
The magazine let go of a columnist who refused to **toe the line** on its new editorial policy.

drill.sentence: In my grandfather's house, everyone {{toed the line}}: dinner at six, no phones at the table and lights out at ten.
drill.hint: obeyed without question (a foot image)

mistake.wrong: He refused to tow the line.
mistake.right: He refused to toe the line.
mistake.why: The verb is *toe*, meaning to touch with your toes, not *tow* (pull); the past tense is *toed*.

entries.related: *fall in line* — start to obey or conform; *follow orders* — do what you're told; *go rogue* — act independently, the opposite.

entries.label: idiom
entries.meaning: Behaving or speaking in a way that is rude, disrespectful or unacceptable in the situation.
entries.usage: Common in arguments, apologies and warnings, usually after *be*: *That was out of line*. It's direct, and *way out of line* makes it stronger. It's about a particular remark or action rather than a person's general character.
examples: Your comment about her weight was totally **out of line**.
I was **out of line** yesterday, and I'm sorry I yelled at you.
The referee said the coach's language was **out of line** and threw him out of the game.

drill.sentence: Calling the waiter an idiot because the soup was cold was way {{out of line}}.
drill.hint: unacceptable (not *uncalled for* or *over the top*)

entries.related: *uncalled for* — unnecessary and unfair; *cross the line* — go beyond what is acceptable; *over the top* — exaggerated or excessive.

entries.label: idiom
entries.meaning: An attempt to satisfy several competing demands or groups at the same time, which needs constant care.
entries.usage: Common in journalism, politics and talk about work and family. Typical adjectives are *delicate*, *difficult*, *constant* and *tricky*. It's sympathetic and admits that a perfect solution isn't possible.
examples: Working full time while caring for my mom is a constant **balancing act**.
The central bank faces **a delicate balancing act** between fighting inflation and protecting jobs.
For a referee, letting the game flow while keeping the players safe is a tricky **balancing act**.

drill.sentence: Choosing where to spend the holidays, with three families who all want us there, is always {{a balancing act}}.
drill.hint: a careful effort to keep everyone satisfied (a tightrope image; not *juggling*)

entries.related: *a juggling act* — managing many tasks at once; *walk a tightrope* — be in a situation where any mistake is dangerous; *a trade-off* — giving up one thing to get another.

entries.label: idiom
entries.meaning: To do something too much or with too much enthusiasm, so that it becomes excessive.
entries.usage: Common in conversation about spending, decorating, gifts, praise and diets, often with *with* or *on* + noun: *Don't go overboard with the salt*. It's light and friendly, typical in advice and in self-criticism.
examples: I **went a little overboard** at the farmers market and bought six kinds of tomatoes.
My parents **go overboard** every Christmas, and the kids end up with way too many presents.
Some critics think the city **went overboard** with its new parking rules.

drill.sentence: When I started running, I {{went overboard}} and signed up for three races in one month.
drill.hint: did too much (a ship image; not *got carried away*)

entries.related: *get carried away* — get so excited that you lose control; *over the top* — exaggerated; *overdo it* — do too much, often physically.

entries.label: idiom
entries.meaning: Excessive or exaggerated, going beyond what is reasonable or appropriate.
entries.usage: Common about decorations, reactions, performances, praise and punishments. It follows *be*, or comes before a noun with hyphens: *an over-the-top wedding*. It can be critical or affectionate, and the short form *OTT* is mainly British.
examples: With gold columns and an indoor waterfall, the hotel lobby was a little **over the top**.
The actor's performance was so **over the top** that the audience started laughing.
A lifetime ban seems **over the top** for a first offense.

drill.sentence: A twelve-course dinner and a live band for a dog's birthday? That's a bit {{over the top}}, even for my neighbors.
drill.hint: excessive (not *much* or *extra*)

entries.related: *go overboard* — do too much; *a bit much* — informal, excessive or annoying; *extra* — slang, overly dramatic.

entries.label: idiom
entries.meaning: To pay for something, especially something expensive, often when you would rather not or when it should not be your cost.
entries.usage: Common in news and conversation, in the pattern *foot the bill for* + thing. It often raises the question of who should pay, so it appears in complaints about costs being passed on: *Who's going to foot the bill?*
examples: Taxpayers will **foot the bill** for the new stadium, even though the team's owner is a billionaire.
My parents offered to **foot the bill** for the wedding, so we didn't argue about the guest list.
When the trip was canceled, employees had to **foot the bill** for their nonrefundable flights.

drill.sentence: We all went out for sushi, and somehow my brother-in-law ended up {{footing the bill}} for twelve people.
drill.hint: paying for everything (a body-part verb; not *picking up the tab*)

entries.related: *pick up the tab* — pay for a meal or a shared cost; *pay through the nose* — pay too much; *split the bill* — share the cost.
entries.origin: From an old use of *foot* meaning to add up an account and write the total at the bottom, or foot, of it.

entries.label: idiom
entries.meaning: A quick, rough calculation made with simple numbers and assumptions, to get an approximate answer.
entries.usage: Common in science, engineering, business and journalism, often to introduce an estimate: *A back-of-the-envelope calculation suggests …* It signals that the number is rough, not precise. *Back-of-the-envelope estimate* and *back-of-the-napkin math* are common variants.
examples: A quick **back-of-the-envelope calculation** shows we'd save about two thousand dollars a year with solar panels.
My **back-of-the-envelope calculation** says the training run will need about three weeks on our cluster.
By one **back-of-the-envelope calculation**, the city needs ten thousand new apartments to bring rents down.

drill.sentence: Before agreeing to the road trip, my dad did {{a back-of-the-envelope calculation}} of what the gas would cost.
drill.hint: a rough, quick estimate (a stationery image)

entries.related: *a ballpark figure* — an approximate number; *a rule of thumb* — a rough practical guideline; *a Fermi estimate* — a rough estimate built from simple assumptions, mainly in science.
